candidates.attacker_control: Server side: any remote, unauthenticated HTTP client that can reach a Camel HTTP consumer (Jetty, Servlet, CamelServlet, and their camel-http4 equivalents) controls both the Content-Type header and the full request body, i.e. fully controls the serialized object graph. Client side: a malicious or compromised HTTP server reached by a Camel HTTP producer controls the response Content-Type and body (relevant when route targets are derived from untrusted input, e.g. CamelHttpUri/bridge endpoints).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The deserialization is a documented Camel capability (Java-object body transfer / transferException), so it is deliberate functionality rather than an accidental typo; however, in this snapshot there is no opt-in flag (searches for allowJavaSerializedObject/allowJava found nothing), no ObjectInputFilter, and no resolveClass/superclass allow-list in the HTTP helpers, and the sibling Netty implementation requires transferException=true, so the unconditional camel-http/camel-http4 behavior is inconsistent with the opt-in pattern. Exploitation also requires the application to expose an HTTP consumer (or call an untrusted URL) and, for RCE, a gadget on the classpath; this was reasoned from source only, not executed, and the association with a specific CVE/fix was not verified in this run (no external lookup, no git history).
candidates.impact: Remote code execution in the JVM running the Camel application (gadget-chain dependent) because the attacker's object graph is deserialized before route logic; at minimum, arbitrary class instantiation/deserialization side effects and denial of service via crafted streams. Because it happens inside the HTTP binding, it precedes and bypasses any route-level authentication, authorization, or message validation. The same primitive on the producer side gives a malicious/compromised HTTP peer code execution in the client application.
candidates.prerequisites: An application that exposes a Camel HTTP consumer endpoint (camel-jetty / camel-servlet / camel-http with its servlet) and uses the default binding, or a route that calls an attacker-influenced URL. For code execution a Java deserialization gadget chain must be on the classpath (e.g. commons-collections 3.2.1, which is a managed dependency in parent/pom.xml and is pulled in by several components); without a gadget the flaw still yields attacker-driven object instantiation/DoS. The exact Content-Type value must be used (JAX-RS/JSON etc. not affected).
candidates.root_cause: Camel's HTTP bindings treat the HTTP Content-Type header as the only gate for Java deserialization. Whenever Content-Type equals "application/x-java-serialized-object", the payload is passed to HttpHelper.deserializeJavaObjectFromStream(), which unconditionally calls new ObjectInputStream(is).readObject(). There is no allowJavaSerializedObject opt-in, no class allow-list/ObjectInputFilter, and no trust check anywhere in the snapshot; the camel-http/camel-http4 request binding is used by Jetty/Servlet/CamelServlet consumers, so the deserialization happens while the inbound message is populated, before any route-level authentication, validation, or choice logic runs. The producer path has the same problem for responses (it deserializes even when the endpoint's transferException option is disabled).
candidates.title: Unauthenticated Java deserialization of HTTP payloads in Camel HTTP components (request body and response body)
candidates.trace: HttpMessage constructor (components/camel-http/.../HttpMessage.java:52) invokes the binding's readRequest() as soon as the request message is built; DefaultHttpBinding.readRequest (camel-http .../DefaultHttpBinding.java:78) checks the request Content-Type, and when it equals application/x-java-serialized-object it converts the body to an InputStream and calls HttpHelper.deserializeJavaObjectFromStream() (lines 137-148). That helper constructs new ObjectInputStream(is) and calls readObject() on the attacker's bytes (camel-http .../helper/HttpHelper.java:128 and 130; camel-http4 equivalent at HttpHelper.java:112 and 114, invoked from http4 DefaultHttpBinding.java:124-135). Producer-side, HttpProducer.extractResponseBody deserializes any response with the same Content-Type without requiring transferException (camel-http .../HttpProducer.java:294-300); camel-ahc has the same helper pattern (AhcHelper.java:72-74 used from DefaultAhcBinding.java:225-229). Notably, camel-netty-http gates its response deserialization on the endpoint's transferException option (NettyHttpHelper.java:139-146), demonstrating that this behavior is meant to be opt-in, which the camel-http/camel-http4 paths are not.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed. Exact gadget availability and whether a given deployment uses the default binding are deployment-dependent. The intended upstream fix (a default-false allowJavaSerializedObject option) could not be confirmed from the snapshot because no patch/history is available.

coverage_summary: B0 tools only (file listing, literal search, bounded reads); 6,614 files visible, 0 excluded by sensitive/binary filters, no precomputed relation index. I inspected the HTTP family in depth (camel-http, camel-http4, camel-jetty-common/jetty9, camel-servlet, camel-netty-http/netty4-http, camel-ahc, camel-spark-rest, camel-restlet), camel-core header filtering/converter/XPath/XSLT/file handling, camel-exec, camel-xmljson, camel-xmlsecurity, camel-saxon, camel-shiro, camel-pgevent, and the parent/assembly POMs (used to date the snapshot to ~March 2015, pre-2.15.0). Coverage is selective, not exhaustive: the snapshot contains ~4,300 component source files; I did not read all of them, no test sources exist in the tree, and no git history or patch information is available.
limitations: No build/test execution, no runtime confirmation, no exploit payloads; findings are source-level leads only.
No internet/CVE database/git history access, so the candidate could not be mapped to a specific CVE or fix commit and the intended ground-truth defect cannot be confirmed.
Test sources and any .git metadata are absent from the snapshot, removing signals (security regression tests, precise commit date) that would normally disambiguate similar issues.
Exploitability of the deserialization candidate depends on deployment facts not visible here (exposed HTTP consumer, default binding, gadget chain on the classpath).
Only a subset of the ~6,600 files was reviewed in depth; uninspected components (e.g. camel-cxf, camel-jms, camel-mail, cloud connectors) may contain stronger issues.

rejected_leads.lead: Missing inbound Camel-header filtering: HttpHeaderFilterStrategy (camel-http:50, camel-http4, camel-netty-http, camel-netty4-http, camel-spark-rest) sets only setOutFilterPattern("(?i)(Camel|org\.apache\.camel)...") while no inFilterPattern is configured, so applyFilterToExternalHeaders in DefaultHeaderFilterStrategy.doFiltering (camel-core .../DefaultHeaderFilterStrategy.java:222-270) lets HTTP request headers such as CamelExecCommandExecutable, CamelFileName, CamelSqlQuery or CamelHttpUri through to downstream components (e.g. DefaultExecBinding.java:50-52), potentially enabling RCE/file-write depending on the route.
rejected_leads.reason: Real and security-relevant, but impact is conditional on a downstream header-driven endpoint (exec/file/sql/http) and the internal 'Camel*' header namespace may be treated as trusted by design; I could not establish that the missing in-filter is the snapshot's intended defect, so it remains a secondary, unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: XML External Entity gaps: camel-core XmlConverter disables only external-general-entities (XmlConverter.java:1104-1110) and leaves parameter entities/DOCTYPE processing enabled, and camel-xmljson XmlJsonDataFormat.doStart (XmlJsonDataFormat.java:62-128) configures no parser security at all (json-lib/XOM parsing).
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible XXE/file-read and DoS exposure, but exploitability depends on parser defaults and, for xmljson, on the optional XOM profile (pom.xml:69-100); I could not confirm a concrete vulnerable path or the applied hardening in this configuration, so it is not the strongest evidence-backed candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Other Java deserialization sinks (camel-shiro ShiroSecurityProcessor.java:119-126; camel-ahc AhcHelper.java:72-74; camel-cassandraql/camel-sql aggregators; camel-javaspace).
rejected_leads.reason: Same weakness class in other components; camel-shiro requires knowledge of the shared passphrase, the aggregator/Javaspace paths require a compromised datastore/space, and AHC is a client-side duplicate of the HTTP issue, so they were not selected as separate candidates (one root cause family was kept).

rejected_leads.lead: camel-file CamelFileName path handling (GenericFileProducer.createFileName, lines 284-359) permits subdirectory/.. names when flatten is false.
rejected_leads.reason: Documented Camel behavior (flatten option exists to strip paths); no evidence this is an unintended defect.

rejected_leads.lead: PgEvent NOTIFY statement built by string concatenation (camel-pgevent PgEventProducer.java:56).
rejected_leads.reason: Data originates from the message body destined for a NOTIFY payload on a fixed configured channel; no demonstrated attacker-controlled SQL execution impact.

summary: B0 review of the Apache Camel 2.15-SNAPSHOT source snapshot (6,614 visible files; main sources/build files only, 0 files excluded by the sensitive/binary filters; no tests present in the tree). I traced the HTTP request/response handling paths and identified one strongest candidate: the Camel HTTP bindings deserialize attacker-supplied Java serialized streams with no opt-in flag, whitelist, or trust check. Related weaker leads (missing inbound Camel-header filtering; XML parser hardening gaps; Shiro token deserialization) are recorded as rejected/unconfirmed. No code was executed and nothing was runtime-confirmed.
